disclaimer: None of these is marked correct. The tower is genuinely disputed: dating ranges from the 1st century CE (mortar analysis) to the 12th century (the Masud ibn Daud inscription — a slab set into the wall later, and not above the entrance).
against: Against

citadel.title: Defensive citadel
citadel.summary: The official UNESCO reading: the tower is part of the defensive system of the walled city.
for: For the 12th century this is not in dispute — the tower is built into the Old City's fortifications.
Walls 5 m thick at the base and narrow slit openings suit a defensive purpose.
The single entrance is raised above ground, as is usual in a fortified tower.
against: It does not account for the lower storeys, which some researchers date to the 7th–6th centuries BCE.
A defensive tower has no need of a 21 m well and an elaborate water-collection system.
The beak-shaped buttress serves no obvious defensive function.

fire-temple.title: Zoroastrian fire temple
fire-temple.summary: D. Akhundov dates the tower to the 7th–6th centuries BCE and reads seven fire outlets at its crown.
for: It accounts for the very early dating of the lower masonry.
Fire worship is well documented on the Absheron peninsula — Ateshgah is the obvious parallel.
It gives the roof platform a purpose that otherwise goes unexplained.
against: The seven fire outlets are not confirmed by excavation.
No soot or burnt layer of the kind a permanent fire would leave is described.
The 7th–6th century BCE dating is itself contested.

dakhma.title: Dakhma — tower of silence
dakhma.summary: A funerary reading: a structure for the Zoroastrian rite of exposing the dead.
for: A tower with an open upper platform matches the dakhma type.
It is consistent with the region's Zoroastrian context.
against: Dakhmas are traditionally placed outside a settlement; this tower stands at its centre.
Eight roofed storeys are redundant for a rite that needs only a platform.
No funerary finds of the kind such a use implies are described.

astronomical.title: Astronomical tower
astronomical.summary: Ahmadov links the 30 lower and 31 upper stone corbels to the days of the month, and the buttress to sunrise at the equinox.
for: The counts of 30 and 31 do match the lengths of months.
The stacked storeys would allow observation from several heights.
against: Tested in this model: measured from the OSM footprint the buttress points at 106.7°, while equinox sunrise is at 90.1° — a discrepancy of 16.6°.
The match at 90° only appears if you take the rounded 'due east' of the prose rather than the measured bearing.
Slits that are narrow outside and flare inward are an aperture for admitting a beam, not a sector for viewing the sky.
No source describes observation of stars.

solar-temple.title: Solar temple
solar-temple.summary: Abbas Islamov claims that at sunrise on the winter solstice the beam enters the central window exactly.
for: The openings really are narrow outside and flare inward, which is how an aperture works.
The observation was recorded photographically by its author in 2004.
against: No source identifies which window is meant, which makes the claim hard to test.

Tested in this model: at sunrise on 21 December the closest match is the slit at the foot of the climb to the roof, about 1° off. It is the only candidate left — the later arched window, which came second at about 2°, was removed from the model on 2026-08-10 when the owner restated that the storeys carry no windows at all. That 1° is a consequence of a placeholder, not a result. Before the change the nearest slit missed by roughly 8°.

The bearing of every opening in the model is set by where the stair starts, and no source fixes that: it is a placeholder. Worse for this test, whether that particular opening exists at all is unrecorded — the owner says some flights have a window at the beginning of the climb and some do not, and which ones has not been asked. The model falls back on a geometric check and says so. The result settles the question neither way.

oil-column.title: Oil distillation column
oil-column.summary: V. Ibragimov proposes an industrial purpose: distilling oil.
for: Absheron has produced oil for centuries; it was gathered here long before the industrial era.
The elaborate system of pipes and channels inside the tower needs explaining.
against: The pipework as described collects water downward rather than drawing off a distillate.
No thermal damage of the kind distillation would leave is described.
The reading has no support in the archaeological literature.

lighthouse.title: Lighthouse
lighthouse.summary: Use of the tower as a lighthouse is documented for the 18th–19th centuries.
for: This is not a hypothesis but a documented fact for that period.
The height and the position by the shoreline suit a lighthouse.
against: It explains a late use only, not the purpose it was built for.
By the time the tower served as a lighthouse it was already many centuries old.
